title: The Fourier Transform and Its Applications, EE 261 — shard 2: Chapters 4–6
access: full (official Stanford Engineering Everywhere PDF; no broad reuse license is stated, so open access does not imply republication rights)
topics: Chapter 4 — Distributions and Their Fourier Transforms
4.1 The Day of Reckoning — limits of L1 Fourier theory; sinc as the motivating failure; the route through Schwartz functions and tempered distributions
4.2 The Right Functions for Fourier Transforms — smoothness versus decay; rapidly decreasing/Schwartz functions; inversion and Parseval on S
4.3 A Very Little on Integrals — absolute integrability, dominated convergence, and power-law tests for decay
4.4 Distributions — limits versus continuous linear functionals; functions inducing distributions; delta as evaluation; compact-support test functions
4.5 A Physical Analogy for Distributions — a thermometer/test-function measurement of a heat distribution
4.6 Limits of Distributions — convergence by pairings; Gaussian, rectangle, and general unit-area approximations to delta
4.7 The Fourier Transform of a Tempered Distribution — transform by dual action; inversion; delta, constant, shifted delta, exponentials, sine, and cosine
4.8 Fluxions Finis — distributional derivatives of steps, ramps, signum, delta, and logarithm
4.9–4.10 Approximation and compatibility — every tempered distribution approximated by Schwartz-function distributions; generalized transform contains the classical transform
4.11–4.17 Operations — reversal and duality; products with smooth functions; derivative, shift, scaling, and convolution theorems; principal-value transforms
4.18 Delta Hard at Work — ideal low-, high-, and notch-filter impulse responses; Fraunhofer diffraction for one slit, two slits, and point sources
4.19–4.21 Appendices — Riemann–Lebesgue lemma; explicit smooth windows; 1/x as a Cauchy principal-value distribution
Chapter 5 — III, Sampling, and Interpolation
5.1 X-Ray Diffraction — crystals as atomic-scale diffraction gratings and reciprocal spacing in crystallography
5.2 The III Distribution — Dirac comb definition; periodizing by convolution; sampling by multiplication; scaling identity
5.3 Fourier Transform of III — Poisson summation; self-transform property; reciprocal comb spacing; crystal electron-density spectra
5.4 Periodic Distributions and Fourier Series — periodicity as shift invariance; Fourier series of III; Fourier transforms of periodic signals
5.5–5.6 Sampling Signals — bandlimitedness; impossibility of simultaneous time and band limitation; Shannon interpolation; Nyquist rate and oversampling
5.7 Interpolation More Generally — shifted sincs as an orthonormal basis; comparison with Lagrange polynomial interpolation
5.8 Finite Sampling — exact reconstruction of a finite Fourier series from 2N+1 samples; periodized-sinc identities
5.9 Troubles with Sampling — finite-record approximation, endpoint ambiguity, undersampling, and aliasing as spectral overlap
5.10–5.11 Appendices — uniqueness of the period-1 self-transforming comb; rigorous time-limited versus bandlimited impossibility
Chapter 6 — Discrete Fourier Transform
6.1–6.3 From Continuous to Discrete — sampled time/frequency grids, Riemann-sum motivation, DFT definition, vector complex exponentials, real-input symmetry, and reciprocal grid spacings
6.4 Gauss's Problem — twelve observations of Pallas fit by a finite Fourier series
6.5–6.7 DFT structure and inversion — periodic indexing; discrete deltas; roots-of-unity orthogonality; reversal, duality, inverse transform, and matrix form
6.8–6.9 DFT properties — Parseval, shifts, modulation, circular convolution, delta identities, and equivalence of any N consecutive index sets
6.10 FFT Algorithm — even/odd splitting, recursive DFT matrix factorization, butterfly stages, NlogN complexity, and bit-reversal sorting
6.11 Zero Padding — preservation of original DFT bins, denser frequency grid, and the condition that padding not erase unknown data
key_results: If f∈L1(R), then Ff exists, is continuous, satisfies |Ff(s)|≤||f||1, and tends to zero as |s|→∞. These facts do not guarantee inversion or that Ff is itself integrable. [§§4.1, 4.19]

The basic pair Π↔sinc exposes the weakness of absolute-integrability theory: Π is in L1, but sinc is not, even though its oscillatory improper transform recovers Π away from the jump endpoints. [§4.1.1, printed pp. 138–140]

The Schwartz space S consists of infinitely differentiable functions whose derivatives decay faster than every power of |x|. The Fourier transform maps S to itself, Fourier inversion holds on S, and Parseval's identity is valid there. [§4.2]

Repeated integration by parts makes the smoothness/decay tradeoff precise: derivatives of f become powers of frequency multiplying Ff, so enough smoothness and boundary decay force rapid spectral decay. [§4.2.1]

A tempered distribution is a continuous linear functional on S: it accepts a Schwartz test function and returns a complex number. Ordinary functions of at most polynomial growth induce tempered distributions by integration against the test function. [§4.4.2–4.4.3]
Delta is defined without assigning it a pointwise infinity: ⟨δ,φ⟩=φ(0), and the shifted distribution satisfies ⟨δa,φ⟩=φ(a). Convolution with delta is the identity, δ*φ=φ. [§§4.4.1–4.4.3]

If fn distributions converge on every test function, their pointwise pairing limit defines a distribution. Any unit-area f yields the delta approximation fp(x)=pf(px)→δ as p→∞; Gaussian and shrinking-rectangle families are special cases. [§§4.6–4.6.1]

The generalized Fourier transform is defined by dual action, ⟨FT,φ⟩=⟨T,Fφ⟩, with the analogous inverse definition. Fourier inversion then holds for every tempered distribution in a few lines because it already holds for Schwartz functions. [§4.7.1]

Generalized transform pairs include Fδ=1, F1=δ, Fδa=e^{−2πisa}, and F(e^{2πiax})=δa. Thus eternal sinusoids acquire discrete line spectra even though their classical Fourier integrals diverge. [§4.7.2]
Under the notes' normalization, F(cos 2πax)=1/2(δa+δ−a) and F(sin 2πax)=1/(2i)(δa−δ−a); the former is real/even and the latter imaginary/odd. [§4.7.2]
The distributional derivative is defined by ⟨T′,φ⟩=−⟨T,φ′⟩, and higher derivatives transfer with alternating sign. Consequently H′=δ, the ramp derivative is H, sgn′=2δ, and ⟨δ′,φ⟩=−φ′(0). [§4.8]

The generalized transform genuinely extends the classical one: whenever f and its classical Ff induce distributions, the distribution induced by Ff equals the generalized transform of the distribution induced by f. [§4.10]
A smooth function can multiply a distribution through ⟨gT,φ⟩=⟨T,gφ⟩. In particular g(x)δa=g(a)δa, so xδ=0; conversely, any distribution T satisfying xT=0 is cδ. [§4.13]
The derivative theorem survives unchanged in form: F(T′)=2πis FT and (FT)′=F(−2πixT). Combined with parity, it gives F(sgn)=1/(πis), with 1/s interpreted as a principal value. [§4.14]
Further principal-value pairs are F(1/x)=−πi sgn(s) and FH=1/2[δ+1/(πis)]. The apparent 1/x function acts by a symmetric Cauchy principal-value pairing near zero. [§4.14.1, §4.21]

For distributions, translation and scaling are defined through their action on oppositely translated or reciprocally scaled test functions. The familiar laws follow: F(τbT)=e^{−2πibs}FT, F(T(ax))=|a|^{−1}(FT)(s/a), and δ(ax)=|a|^{−1}δ(x). [§§4.15–4.16]

Convolution is not defined for every pair of distributions, but a test function ψ may convolve with a distribution T, and F(ψ*T)=(Fψ)(FT). Delta identities include δa*δb=δa+b and δ^(n)*f=f^(n). [§4.17]

Ideal high-pass and notch impulse responses require delta terms: high(t)=δ(t)−2νc sinc(2νct), while a symmetric notch centered at ±ν0 has notch(t)=δ(t)−4νc cos(2πν0t)sinc(2νct). Both act by subtracting selected content from the original signal. [§4.18.1]

Under the Fraunhofer far-field approximation, the complex electric field versus p=sinθ/λ is proportional to the Fourier transform of the aperture A(x); observed intensity is proportional to |FA|². [§4.18.2]

A slit of width a produces intensity a²sinc²(a sinθ/λ). Two width-a slits separated by b multiply that envelope by 4cos²(πb sinθ/λ), while two point sources leave only the cosine-squared fringes. [§4.18.2, printed pp. 203–205]

A smooth compact window can be built explicitly from flat exponential pieces and scaled to cut off a signal without introducing endpoint discontinuities; the notes use this to justify inversion and approximation arguments. [§4.20]
The Dirac comb IIIp=Σkδ(x−kp) has two complementary actions: f*IIIp=Σkf(x−kp) periodizes by addition, while f·IIIp=Σkf(kp)δ(x−kp) samples at spacing p. [§§5.2.1–5.2.2]
Comb scaling obeys III(px)=p^{−1}III1/p(x) for p>0. This reciprocal scaling is the first sign that a lattice and its frequency-domain counterpart have inverse spacings. [§5.2.3]
Poisson summation states Σkφ(k)=ΣkFφ(k) for Schwartz φ. It implies the central identity FIII=III and, after scaling, FIIIp=p^{−1}III1/p. [§5.3]

A one-dimensional crystal density ρp=ρ*IIIp transforms to (Fρ/p)III1/p. Diffraction spots therefore sample the atomic form factor at spacing 1/p, so measured spot spacing is reciprocal—not directly proportional—to atomic spacing. [§5.3.1]
A distribution is p-periodic when τpS=S. Periodizing one period φ=ΠpΦ gives Φ=φ*IIIp, and Fourier transformation yields the usual Fourier-series coefficients as samples of Fφ at k/p. [§5.4]

A signal is bandlimited to bandwidth p when its transform vanishes outside |s|<p/2. No nonzero signal can be both time-limited and bandlimited; in fact a bandlimited signal zero on any open interval is identically zero. [§5.5.1, §§5.6 and 5.11]
For a signal with Ff(s)=0 on |s|≥p/2, exact Shannon interpolation is f(t)=Σk f(k/p)sinc[p(t−k/p)]. The sample spacing is 1/p and reconstruction uses infinitely many samples. [§5.6]

If the nonzero spectrum reaches ±νmax, reconstruction requires a sampling rate greater than 2νmax; oversampling replaces p by any larger q and supplies more closely spaced samples than strictly necessary. [§5.6]

The shifted functions {sinc(t−n)} form an orthonormal basis for L2 signals bandlimited to [−1/2,1/2]. Each sample g(n) is exactly the projection ⟨g,sinc(t−n)⟩, making interpolation an orthogonal expansion rather than merely curve fitting. [§5.7]

A q-periodic finite Fourier series with harmonics −N through N is determined by M=2N+1 samples spaced q/M apart. Its exact sampling rate is 2νmax+νmin, and its interpolation kernel is a ratio of sincs. [§5.8]

The periodized-sinc identity Σk sinc(pt−kpq)=[1/(pq)]sin((2N+1)πt/q)/sin(πt/q), with N the largest integer below pq/2, converts an infinite sampling sum into a finite Fourier kernel. The special case Σn sinc(t−n)=1 is highlighted. [§5.8]

Aliasing is the failure of Ff=Πq(Ff*IIIq) when the sampling rate q is below bandwidth: shifted spectral replicas overlap before cutoff. Distinct signals then have identical samples and cannot be distinguished from those samples alone. [§5.9.1]
At one sample per second, cos(9πt/2) aliases to cos(πt/2): their integer samples agree because the original 9/4-Hz line folds to 1/4 Hz after periodization. [§5.9.1, printed pp. 238–241]

Sampling exactly at an endpoint can be signal-dependent: sin(2πt) sampled at 2 Hz can alias to zero, while cos(2πt) at the same rate is recoverable when boundary deltas are cut with half weight. The notes recommend treating such endpoint cases separately. [§5.9.2]
Up to scale, III is uniquely characterized as a period-1 tempered distribution that equals its Fourier transform; normalizing its zeroth Fourier coefficient to one makes it unique. [§5.10]

Starting with an approximately time-limited and bandlimited signal, N=2BL samples and Riemann-sum discretization motivate the DFT. Time and frequency grids satisfy ΔtΔν=1/N, so for fixed N refining one grid coarsens the other. [§§6.1 and 6.3]
For f[0],…,f[N−1], the DFT is F[m]=Σ_{n=0}^{N−1}f[n]e^{−2πimn/N}. It is a linear map CN→CN whose matrix entries are powers of the Nth root of unity. [§§6.2 and 6.5]

DFT inputs and outputs extend naturally as N-periodic sequences, and the transform can be computed over any N consecutive indices. Honest negative indices map by periodicity to bins N/2+1 through N−1. [§§6.6 and 6.9]
For real input and even N, the DFT has conjugate symmetry: bins above N/2 mirror the positive-frequency bins, F[0] is the sample sum, and F[N/2] is the real alternating sample sum. [§6.2.1]
The discrete delta and roots of unity satisfy Fδk=ω^{−k}, F(ω^k)=Nδk, and ω^k·ω^l=N when k≡l mod N and zero otherwise. These orthogonality relations give the inverse DFT. [§§6.7.1–6.7.2]
DFT duality is F(f−)=(Ff)− and FFf=Nf−. Therefore F−1f=(1/N)F(f−)=(1/N)(Ff)−, or f[n]=(1/N)ΣkF[k]e^{2πikn/N}. As matrices, F*F=NI. [§§6.7.3–6.7.5]
DFT Parseval is (Ff)·(Fg)=N(f·g), hence ||Ff||²=N||f||². Shift and modulation dualize as F(τpf)=ω^{−p}Ff and F(ω^nf)=τn(Ff). [§6.8]
Discrete convolution is circular: (f*g)[m]=Σ_{k=0}^{N−1}f[k]g[m−k], with indices modulo N, and F(f*g)=(Ff)(Fg). Conversely, F(fg)=N^{−1}(Ff*Fg). [§6.8.1]
The radix-2 FFT splits the DFT into transforms of even and odd indexed inputs, then recombines them with twiddle factors: F[m]=E[m]+ωN^{−m}O[m] and F[m+N/2]=E[m]−ωN^{−m}O[m]. [§6.10.1]

Recursively factoring N=2^n transforms gives C(N)=2C(N/2)+KN and therefore C(N)=KNlog2N, instead of order N². For N=1024 the notes compare roughly one million direct operations with about ten thousand FFT-scale operations. [§6.10.2]

Radix-2 input sorting is bit reversal: write each index in fixed-width binary, reverse its bits, and feed the corresponding sample into that slot. Butterfly matrices then perform the staged recombinations. [§6.10.3]

If an N-point sequence is padded to M=kN, every original DFT bin survives as F[m]=G[km], while the frequency-grid spacing shrinks by 1/k without changing total frequency extent. Padding refines sampled display points; it is justified only when the omitted time samples are truly zero. [§6.11]
pedagogy: A proof-driven but deliberately conversational bridge from continuous Fourier analysis to computation. Osgood repeatedly starts from a failure or physical question—sinc's nonabsolute integral, an impulse, diffraction, crystal spots, reconstruction from samples, or the cost of a DFT—and then engineers definitions that make the desired operation legitimate. The recurring rule ‘try a function first’ derives distributional operations from integration before elevating the outcome to a definition. Formal proofs are supplied for central identities such as generalized inversion, Poisson summation, sampling, DFT inversion, and FFT complexity, while hard topology, convergence, and existence results are explicitly quarantined or stated without proof. Optional appendices carry rigor on integration, principal values, smooth windows, endpoint behavior, and time/band limitation. The prose uses humor, historical asides, engineering warnings, and frequent prompts to draw or verify small cases. Figures are mostly schematic graphs and transform-domain constructions meant to be reproduced, not polished illustrations. There are no end-of-chapter exercise sets in this shard, but the notes frequently assign short derivations and computational checks and assume concurrent problem sets. Prerequisites are calculus and differential equations, complex exponentials, Fourier series and the classical transform, convolution, elementary probability/physics intuition, linear algebra, geometric series, and comfort with Matlab-style vectors and indexing.

gems: The chapter's crisis is the field's most basic pair: Π transforms cleanly to sinc, yet sinc is not absolutely integrable. Osgood asks how multibillion-dollar industries can depend on integrals that do not converge, then rebuilds the theory instead of hiding the issue. [§4.1.1]

‘Distributions are what distributions do’ becomes a programming interface: pass a distribution a Schwartz function and it returns a number. Delta is no longer an infinite spike but the simplest nontrivial functional—evaluate at zero. [§§4.4.2–4.4.3]
The heat kernel gives delta a job before giving it mystique: as t→0+, the Gaussian solution operator g(·,t)*f tends to δ*f=f and recovers the initial temperature of an infinite rod. [§4.4.1]

Osgood calls limits-based distributions ‘vacuum tubes’ and linear-functional distributions ‘transistors’; the analogy marks a real conceptual upgrade from hazy limiting objects to precise operations on test functions. [§4.4]

Generalized Fourier inversion—the result motivating the entire chapter—takes only a few lines once the transform is defined by ⟨FT,φ⟩=⟨T,Fφ⟩. The right definition makes the hard theorem nearly automatic. [§4.7.1]

Distributional calculus vindicates the student's forbidden answer: the cornered unit ramp really does differentiate to the unit step, and the unit step differentiates to delta. A jump of height two in signum produces 2δ. [§4.8]
The identity g(x)δa=g(a)δa turns a spike into an exact sampler, while δa*δb=δa+b turns spike location into arithmetic under convolution. [§§4.13.1 and 4.17]

Ideal high-pass filtering is literally ‘original minus low-pass part’: its impulse response δ−sinc makes the verbal design visible in one equation. The notch filter repeats the same logic after modulating the sinc to ±ν0. [§4.18.1]

Fraunhofer diffraction makes the transform observable: the aperture is the time-domain signal, angle divided by wavelength is frequency, and visible brightness is the squared magnitude. A single slit displays sinc² ‘live.’ [§4.18.2]
A point aperture predicts a uniformly illuminated far field, giving an optical interpretation of Fδ=1 rather than just a distributional proof. [§4.18.2, printed p. 205]

Von Laue's 1912 proposal tested three hypotheses at once—X-rays are waves, crystals are periodic, and atomic spacing is about 10−8 cm—by using the crystal itself as the grating that could not be manufactured. [§5.1]

The book calls FIII=III ‘the deepest fact about the integers’ known to every engineer and spectroscopist. Periodicity, sampling, Poisson summation, and reciprocal lattices all collapse into that one self-transform. [§5.3]
The reciprocal-lattice warning is intentionally career-sized: mistake diffraction-spot spacing for direct atomic spacing rather than 1/p and ‘kiss your Nobel prize goodbye.’ [§5.3.1]

The sampling theorem proof is only three moves—periodize the spectrum, cut back to the original, invert—and Osgood remarks on the almost obscene efficiency with which multiplication and convolution swap roles. [§5.6]

Shifted sinc functions are not just interpolation bumps; they are an orthonormal basis, and the sample g(n) is the basis coefficient. This connects Shannon reconstruction directly back to Fourier-series projection. [§5.7]

The finite sampling formula writes cos 2πt using three sample values and a forbidding ratio of sinc functions, then a plot confirms the identity. The deliberately absurd complexity makes exact finite reconstruction memorable. [§5.8, printed p. 234]

The identity Σn sinc(t−n)=1 looks impossible term by term; a ±100 partial sum plot exposes Gibbs-like edge effects while the distributional/periodization argument explains the infinite result. [§5.8, printed p. 235]

Aliasing is shown with an exact ambush: a 9/4-Hz cosine sampled once per second is indistinguishable from a 1/4-Hz cosine, and the frequency-domain derivation shows precisely which shifted deltas land inside the reconstruction window. [§5.9.1]

The endpoint pair sin 2πt and cos 2πt makes ‘sample above twice the highest frequency’ more than pedantry: at exactly 2 Hz the sine disappears into all-zero samples while the cosine survives through half-weight boundary deltas. [§5.9.2]

The DFT begins by admitting an impossibility: computation pretends a signal is both time- and band-limited and that finitely many samples suffice. It works well enough that much of the world's economy depends on the approximation. [Chapter 6 opening; §6.1]

Gauss had twelve Pallas orbit measurements and devised the heart of an FFT-style decomposition roughly a century before Cooley and Tukey; the notes give the raw data, fitted coefficients, and modern reconstruction. [§6.4]

Merge-sort is the computational warm-up for FFT: recycling partial work changes one million squared comparisons at N=10^6 into only millions-scale NlogN work, preparing the same divide-and-conquer idea for transforms. [§6.10]
For N=1024, direct DFT scale is about 2^20≈one million operations while FFT scale is about 1024·10≈ten thousand, or roughly five thousand for real inputs. [§6.10.2]

Bit reversal turns a mysterious shuffle into a three-step rule. For N=8, reversing binary indices sends the natural order to 0,4,2,6,1,5,3,7, exactly the order needed by the butterfly stages. [§6.10.3]

Zero padding gets a careful warning: it inserts denser frequency-grid samples and preserves old bins, but it is legitimate only if the newly asserted time samples are truly zero; otherwise it destroys real data rather than adding information. [§6.11]
